item.research_question: How does the presence of local chemical order (LCO) influence the formation, evolution, and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters in equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys compared to a random solid solution?
item.material_system: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) in two states: water-quenched (approximated as a random solid solution, RSS) and aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h (LCO CrCoNi); pure Ni used as a benchmark.
item.processing_route: Raw ingot homogenized at 1,200 °C for 48 h; split into two treatments: (1) water quenched to room temperature to form RSS; (2) aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling to induce LCO. Ion irradiation performed in situ at 300 K using 50 keV He+ ions. Atomistic simulations prepared RSS by random distribution and LCO via MD/MC at 1,300 K with variance-constrained semigrand canonical ensemble.
item.test_conditions: In situ TEM irradiation at 300 K with 50 keV He+ ions up to 1.0 dpa; MD simulations of primary damage with PKA energies of 5, 10, 20, and 40 keV; diffusion simulations at various temperatures (including 1,200 K) to measure vacancy and interstitial mobility.
key_findings: The areal fraction of LCO regions is approximately 3% in water-quenched RSS CrCoNi versus ~30% in the 1,000 °C-aged LCO CrCoNi.
At a low irradiation dose of 0.16 dpa, the LCO sample is nearly defect-free while the RSS sample already contains visible defect clusters.
The number density of defect clusters in the LCO sample is significantly smaller than in the RSS sample across the entire dose range of 0.16 to 1.0 dpa.
The average activation energy for interstitial diffusion increases from 0.22 eV in RSS to 0.34 eV in LCO, while for vacancies it increases from 0.69 eV to 0.76 eV.
The difference in activation energy between interstitial and vacancy diffusion narrows from 0.47 eV in RSS to 0.42 eV in LCO, reducing the mobility ratio.
The correlation factor for interstitial diffusion decreases by 29% (from 0.232 to 0.165) in LCO compared to RSS, indicating stronger localization of interstitial motion.
Large-sized defect clusters (Ncluster > 30) are suppressed in LCO CrCoNi, with the number of point defects in large clusters being ~35% lower than in RSS.

The recombination rate of Frenkel pairs at the end of the thermal spike is nearly identical for RSS and LCO (~99.6%), but the LCO sample retains fewer surviving FPs due to enhanced recombination during the cooling phase.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that LCO enhances irradiation resistance through a two-pronged kinetic effect: (1) it increases migration energy barriers, slowing down the diffusion of both vacancies and interstitials (localizing their motion); and (2) it narrows the mobility ratio between interstitials and vacancies (by affecting interstitials more strongly), which increases the probability of their recombination and annihilation during the cooling phase of the collision cascade, thereby reducing the number of surviving defects and large clusters.
item.limitations: The study notes that small-sized defect clusters (Ncluster < 8) are not detectable by in-situ TEM due to resolution limits and are susceptible to dissolution, so the comparison between experiment and simulation focuses on large-sized clusters. The extent of LCO investigated is limited to chemical short-range order (CSRO) developed via the specific aging treatment.
item.future_work: The authors propose that tailoring composition and heat treatment to extend LCO beyond CSRO into medium-range or long-range order, or adding interstitial alloying elements (such as C, N) with chemical affinity for specific constituents, could further boost irradiation tolerance.
quotes: increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination.
the presence of LCO can effectively inhibit the formation of defect clusters in the early stage of irradiation (up to 1.0 dpa).

LCO increases the energy barriers for defect diffusion, lowering the mobility of the two types of point defects. Consequently, the slower diffusion of the vacancies and interstitials, in particular the reduced difference in their mobility, renders these defects more likely to recombine.
